item.title: For Clues About How A.I. Will Change Work, Look to the Past
item.description:
In December 1931, economists gathered in Washington to discuss the threat that technology posed to American workers.

Switchboard operators were being rendered obsolete by the dial telephone. Movie-theater musicians were superfluous in the age of “talkies.” Teamsters — men driving teams of horses — were losing their jobs to drivers of gasoline-powered trucks.

Such disruptions were nothing new, the economists conceded. But with the Great Depression raging, the risks to the economy and social stability seemed greater than ever. And it was all happening “more rapidly than in any previous age,” warned Sumner H. Slichter, a Harvard economist.

“And yet we have failed, for the most part, to recognize that change presents a major social problem,” he told colleagues at the annual meeting of the American Economic Association.

Nearly a century later, a new generation of economists is trying to make sense of the consequences of another technology: artificial intelligence. And while the jobs they are focused on are different — computer programmers instead of telephone operators, scriptwriters instead of movie musicians, drivers of trucks powered by diesel, not animals — many of the questions they are asking are the same.

Would the undeniable benefits of technology be enjoyed broadly, or accrue only to the wealthy few? Would new jobs emerge in time to replace the ones being destroyed? Was government data up to the task of measuring the rapidly changing economy? And, most importantly, what could the government do to slow these disruptions, or at least to help the workers caught in their wake?

“Technological changes may be so rapid and so far-reaching that they bring about a condition in which all factors of production may be simultaneously unemployed,” Ewan Clague, an economist who later served as commissioner of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, told colleagues in 1931. He even proposed a policy that would not seem out of place in today’s A.I. debate: “Might it not be possible to work out a method of taxing machinery and equipment which would tend to slow down their development?”

Modern economists are revisiting these earlier eras to find lessons relevant to policymakers today. Why did mechanization in the textile industry create widespread unemployment among spinners but not among weavers? Why were the protests that workers staged against industrialization in the 19th century more violent in France than in England? (And why did other technological changes draw little protest at all?)

Why, in short, have some episodes of technological upheaval gone relatively well for workers, and others so badly?

Historical examples are particularly useful right now, economists argue, because this moment is so uncertain. The models that economists typically rely on offer an almost comically broad range of potential outcomes, from a modest productivity boost on a par with that of the internet to “an unprecedented transformation of our economy, larger than the Industrial Revolution, but unfolding over a vastly shorter time frame,” as nearly 200 economists warned in a recent letter.

History won’t provide a definitive answer, said Ben Schneider, an economist at the University of Oslo who studies how technology affects workers. But it can offer a window into the way societies have handled previous periods of rapid change.

“We can look to the past and we can say, well, the implications of the steam engine have basically played out by now,” Mr. Schneider said.

When the economists met in Washington in 1931, unemployment was nearly 20 percent, and would hit 25 percent within a year, which remains a record.

Worries about technology’s taking jobs predated the Depression, but the crisis made them more acute. When telephone companies began replacing manual switchboards with dial telephones in the 1920s, tens of thousands of jobs disappeared. But most of the displaced workers — overwhelmingly young women — found other jobs relatively quickly.

“During the period of business expansion before 1929, technological displacement led directly to relatively little unemployment,” economists at the Bureau of Labor Statistics wrote in a 1932 report, “The Dial Telephone and Unemployment.”

The Depression changed everything. Women who lost their jobs connecting calls had little hope of finding work elsewhere. There were similar challenges in manufacturing, where automation allowed factories to produce steel, car parts and other goods with far fewer workers.

“How empty a modern steel mill seems!” The New York Times Magazine lamented in 1938. “There is something ominous about this — ominous because of the short cuts to come.”

A few years later, however, those mills were producing steel for the American war effort, and with men off fighting, labor-saving technology was a boon rather than a threat. And in the economic boom in the decades after World War II, concerns about technological displacement were mitigated by the abundant job opportunities — many of them tied to designing, manufacturing and selling cars, televisions and washing machines for a growing middle class — that ensured that many displaced workers could find new jobs relatively quickly.

A century earlier, the same pattern had played out in reverse, with much worse outcomes for workers. Landowners in England adopted threshing machines to fill in for scarce human labor when agricultural workers were off fighting Napoleon. When men returned from war, they found that a critical source of work — threshing accounted for as much as half of a rural laborer’s income during the winter months — had evaporated.

What followed were the “Swing Riots,” a wave of unrest in 1830s England that surpassed the better-known protests of the Luddites.

The state of the broader economy, in other words, plays a critical role in deciding how workers will fare when technology disrupts their livelihoods. Timing matters. So does geography — it’s better to lose a job in a region that is thriving than in one that is struggling.

Violent protests against the adoption of threshing machines were much more common in remote areas, said Bruno Caprettini, an economist who has studied the uprising. Closer to cities, where workers could seek other employment, protests were less intense. And by the mid-19th century, as the economy improved and wages rose, protests died down as workers found better-paying jobs.

“Nobody misses manual threshing,” Mr. Caprettini said. What they missed was the stability that threshing provided. If workers have other opportunities, they will adapt. If they don’t, they will protest, or even revolt.

One reason workers were hit so hard by automation during the first Industrial Revolution and in the 1930s is that their jobs disappeared so quickly — literally overnight in the case of telephone operators. Phone companies typically made the transition from manual to mechanized dialing at midnight on a Saturday, when call volumes were low. Operators who had jobs when they went home on Friday were out of work by Monday morning.

Such rapid changes gave workers little time to adapt. Not only were women who lost their jobs as telephone operators less likely to be working in the telephone industry a decade later, they were less likely to be working at all, according to a 2024 study. And those who did have jobs tended to earn lower wages than before the switch to dial phones.

In industries where the transitions were more gradual, workers tended to fare better.

By the time gasoline-powered passenger cars became prevalent in the 1900s, for example, it was clear that the technology would eventually come for delivery trucks. But it was only after World War I that motor trucks displaced horse-drawn wagons en masse. The number of teamsters actually rose from 1900 to 1910, then declined gradually in the 1910s before dropping precipitously in the 1920s and ’30s.

The relatively slow transition allowed young men, recognizing there was no future in driving horses, to pursue other industries. That left a shortage of drivers, which meant that wages actually rose for the mostly older workers who stuck around to finish out their careers.

Something similar may be happening today as modern drivers face a new technological disruption: self-driving trucks. That threat, too, has been clear for years, and there are signs that younger workers have become more reluctant to enter the industry, said Kevin Lang, an economist at Boston University.

But while truckers have had some warning, A.I. appears to be threatening jobs that until recently seemed relatively safe from technological upheaval, such as software development and legal services. That, too, has echoes of the 1930s, said Amy Bix, a historian at Iowa State University.

“There really was a deep set of concerns in the Depression era that technology was advancing faster than society’s ability to adjust, and that people were sort of being left to fend for themselves in the wreckage,” she said. “Today, you really do have a very similar sense of uncertainty and fear that these technological changes are all coming so rapidly.”

The A.I. debate, like earlier episodes of technological change, tends to focus on the threat of job losses. But economists say the true impact is often subtler. Technology sometimes costs jobs, they say, but it almost always changes them.

In 1851, about 220,000 people worked as boot makers in England. The number hardly changed over the next six decades, rising and falling only modestly before settling at about 207,000 in 1911.

“If you look just at that, you might think, OK, not that much has happened in this industry,” said Hillary Vipond, an economic historian.

In fact, the industry changed entirely over that period. The boot makers of the mid-19th century were artisans, working in towns throughout England. The boot makers of the early-20th century were factory workers in cities, producing far more boots per hour at far lower prices than their artisan predecessors.

The episode carries several lessons, Ms. Vipond said. Technology made workers more productive, but that didn’t result in a loss of jobs, because lower prices led to increased demand — a phenomenon known as “Jevon’s paradox.” More people could afford boots; owners of one pair could now buy several.

But while the number of jobs didn’t fall, the work changed. That is what often gets missed in discussions of technological disruption, Ms. Vipond said: Technologies destroy jobs, but they also create new ones. By one estimate, roughly 60 percent of jobs in the United States in 2018 were in occupations that didn’t exist in 1940.

“We don’t focus enough on the new jobs,” she said. “The reason this hasn’t been a crisis before is because in every decade we have seen new jobs emerge.”

Still, Ms. Vipond said, just because new jobs eventually emerge doesn’t mean that transitions are easy for workers. The Industrial Revolution displaced so many workers so rapidly that it crushed wages for decades — a period known as “Engel’s Pause” — before demand caught up with supply and workers’ living standards began improving again.

Even shorter disruptions can be painful for the workers caught in the crossfire, said Mr. Schneider, the University of Oslo economist. Losing a job and being unemployed is costly for workers and their families, even if they eventually find another.

“It’s easy for us today to look back and say, yeah, there was some disruption, but basically, in the end, it was worth it,” Mr. Schneider said. “And maybe for us it was worth it. But for the people at the time, it might not have felt like it was worth it for them.”

Most economists don’t give much credence to predictions that A.I. will mean the end of work. But the disruptions it causes could dwarf past episodes. The A.I. revolution is also global, affecting not just the rich economies where the technology is being developed, but also poorer countries that have built their economies partly on call centers, tech support and other back-office industries that could be vulnerable to technological upheaval.

Mr. Lang, the Boston University economist, said that if A.I. wipes out a large share of white-collar jobs, it isn’t clear what would replace them.

“I have colleagues who say we’ve been worried the world is going to collapse many times in the past, and it never has,” Mr. Lang said. “To which my response is, I’ve been sick many times, but I’ve never died.”

item.title: How Trump Gave the Worst Polluters a Free Pass
item.description:
Middle schoolers on their way to class in the shadow of a flare from the Indorama Ventures chemical facility in Port Neches, Texas. Video by Meridith Kohut.

Supported by

The president temporarily waived clean-air rules for industrial facilities that spew cancer-causing gases. Then his appointees worked to gut the regulations altogether.

By Eric Lipton and Maxine Joselow

Graphics by Mira Rojanasakul

Eric Lipton reported from Port Neches, Texas. Maxine Joselow reported from Clairton, Pa., and Richmond, Va.

Within sight of a southeast Texas middle school stands a chemical plant that President Trump excused from new federal rules intended to curb its cancer-causing pollution.

About a 30-minute drive from Pittsburgh, a steel-making facility has spewed carcinogenic chemicals near homes for years. Mr. Trump gave it a similar waiver from recent clean-air rules.

And on the outskirts of Richmond, Va., the owners of an industrial warehouse emailed the Trump administration asking for their own waiver. Their wish was granted. Nine months later, the facility accidentally released a large plume of carcinogenic gas into the community.

In total, since taking office again, Mr. Trump exempted 202 facilities in 39 states and Puerto Rico from clean-air regulations that were going into effect. Some were among the country’s worst industrial polluters, including chemical manufacturers, copper smelters and coal-burning power plants. About 3.3 million people live within three miles of at least one affected facility.

Note: The number of people near each facility was determined using the 2024 population in each census block-group within a three-mile radius of each plant. Block-groups that were partly within the radius were population-weighted with 2020 census block population counts. Source: Data from the Environmental Defense Fund and Environmental Integrity Project. The New York Times

The exemptions represent the biggest presidential intervention in enforcement of the Clean Air Act in the half-century since President Richard M. Nixon signed the bedrock environmental law. And that is only one of the ways the Trump administration is dismantling a variety of federal environmental protections.

Before Mr. Trump’s return, the chemical industry was losing its fight to block or at least delay tougher E.P.A. requirements to reduce toxic emissions. It had pleaded with agency officials, filed lawsuits and appealed to Congress. But officials and the courts had largely rejected the industry’s claims of undue expense and regulatory overreach.

Now, Mr. Trump is prioritizing the economic interests of corporations and easing costs for polluting industries, and their immense clout is striking.

The president’s exemptions were good for two years, with the possibility of an extension. The reprieve for the companies gave Mr. Trump time to stock the Environmental Protection Agency with appointees who had lobbied for the industries they now regulate. Those officials then quickly went to work from the inside to gut the rules altogether.

Mr. Trump has taken an expansive view of executive power in his second term. On the environmental front, he has unilaterally shredded regulations, withheld science funding appropriated by Congress and ordered coal plants that planned to shutter to continue running.

Even so, his evisceration of the new Clean Air Act rules stands out.

Many of the details of how the Trump administration aided the chemical industry are being reported here for the first time. In one upside-down moment, industry executives provided the agenda for a meeting with E.P.A. staff and then effectively presided over it.

Mr. Trump also nominated Aaron Szabo, a former lobbyist for the Advanced Medical Technology Association, or AdvaMed, a powerful trade group, to lead the E.P.A.’s air regulation office. Once there, Mr. Szabo helped handle the waiver requests and then pushed employees to pull back on enforcement, documents show.

To understand how Mr. Trump gave a free pass to some of the worst polluters, The New York Times reviewed more than 10,000 pages of government documents and spoke to more than 70 people familiar with the efforts, including former E.P.A. officials and industry executives.

“These companies, with their campaign contributions and the revolving door of former lobbyists and executives that now work in the regulatory agencies — that is where the petrochemical industry gets its power,” said Brent Coon, a Beaumont, Texas, lawyer who has spent decades squaring off in court against petrochemical firms over environmental and health risks.

The Clean Air Act requires the E.P.A. — created in 1970 to protect public health and the environment — to periodically review the latest pollution controls and impose them broadly if they are affordable and effective. The most recent review began under the Biden administration, which in 2024 finalized new, tougher requirements.

In granting the waivers to those rules, Mr. Trump cited an obscure clause in the act that allows exemptions if complying with new rules would threaten national security and if the necessary technology is not widely available.

Yet the president approved the waivers even though the equipment was readily accessible and the industry’s national security claims had little detail to substantiate them, documents show.

The Biden administration pushed through the new pollution requirements after evidence emerged about the health threats posed by ethylene oxide, a colorless gas used to make products like plastic soda bottles and to sterilize medical devices like pacemakers.

E.P.A. researchers had concluded that ethylene oxide was 30 to 60 times as carcinogenic as previously thought, particularly for people who live near plants where the gas is made or used. The agency held meetings to warn community members about the elevated risks.

Outside Richmond, home to one of the country’s largest commercial sterilizers of medical devices, some residents left one of these briefings wondering whether recent cancer diagnoses among neighbors were tied to the plant, though it is virtually impossible to prove pollution caused a specific cancer case.

“You see these pretty buildings, and you think they’re OK,” said Wayne Powell, who lives a five-minute drive from the plant, which resembles an ordinary warehouse. “But you don’t know that they’re harboring things that are hazardous to our health.”

As recently as April, the plant, owned by Sterilization Services of Virginia, had a mishap. A faulty valve caused 580 pounds of ethylene oxide to leak from large drums and waft in a toxic plume over nearby homes, state records show. The plant’s state permit allows it to discharge no more than 400 pounds of ethylene oxide in an entire year.

Representatives for Sterilization Services of Virginia did not respond to calls seeking comment.

The new rules required not only sterilizers but also chemical plants and steel facilities to monitor for emissions of cancer-causing gases along their property lines by 2027. If certain amounts of the gases got out, the operators had to fix the leaks. Some facilities also had to build special containment systems — akin to giant breadboxes — to reduce gas releases.

Though the facilities would still have to follow pollution limits already in place, the industries fought the E.P.A.’s new mandates, calling them expensive, unnecessary and unworkable. They also challenged the Biden administration’s scientific findings.

“It is critical that regulation of our industry is based on sound science and that those regulations reflect a reasonable assessment of the risks and benefits involved,” Brendan Bradley, a spokesman for the American Chemistry Council, an industry trade group, said in a statement.

The Trump administration did not ask companies to present an exhaustive case for why they deserved a waiver from these new requirements. It was as easy as sending an email to the E.P.A. and invoking the obscure exemption language in the act, a provision that no president had ever used.

Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement the waivers were necessary to protect American manufacturing.

“Exemptions were issued due to crushing Biden-era regulations that required large swaths of our industrial base to adopt technologies that don’t exist outside the imagination of Biden’s E.P.A. bureaucrats,” she said.

Mr. Trump’s decisions rewarded industries that backed his re-election campaign and continued to donate to his pet causes once he won.

AdvaMed boasted earlier this year in a letter to members that its lobbying efforts, which included political contributions to Mr. Trump’s causes, had paid off, saving the industry millions of dollars in upgrades.

“Membership has its privileges,” the group wrote.

The chemical plant in Port Neches, Texas, just south of the meandering Neches River, is a vital cog in American manufacturing. It is among the country’s biggest producers of ethylene oxide.

The plant’s owner, Indorama Ventures, is a major employer in the region and supports local schools, including Groves Middle School. It provides a football training complex through which its chemical pipelines run. It also sponsors the annual Fish-O-Rama Fishing Tournament to raise money for local science and math programs.

The plant also has a long history of releasing toxic pollutants into the community, state records show.

On more than 500 occasions since 2003, it has experienced malfunctions or other failures that resulted in releases of air pollution or toxic chemicals, frequently in violation of its permit, Texas records show.

From his front yard, dotted with baseballs and children's bikes, Cody Coburn can see the flares that burn off excess toxic gases from the plant across the street. Some nights they rattle his windows, suggesting a possible malfunction at the plant.

The incidents leave Mr. Coburn and his wife wondering if they are taking a risk living there with their young sons. “We’ve talked about moving away,” he said.

The violations continued after Indorama, based in Bangkok, purchased the facility from the Texas-based Huntsman Corporation in 2020.

A particularly alarming incident occurred in early 2022. A control valve failed, sending 57,000 pounds of pollutants into the air, including ethylene oxide, records show. The discharges continued for nearly a week.

That 2022 incident, and others like it, put Indorama on the radar of E.P.A. officials who were rewriting the rules for chemical plants.

These kinds of facilities had long used models to estimate their emissions. The problem was, no one could say if the estimates were accurate.

The E.P.A. decided to find out. The agency emailed the managers of the Indorama plant and 10 other facilities, ordering them to install temporary devices at the edges of their properties to measure toxins in the air.

Career E.P.A. employees were stunned by the results, said Brenda Shine, then the agency engineer who supervised the data collection.

Based on data provided by the plant, agency staff had estimated the tests for benzene, a gas linked to cancer, would find about 0.02 micrograms per cubic meter of air — a relatively small amount. But the actual air sampling revealed benzene levels nearly 50 times as high. It also found three times as much ethylene oxide in the air as estimated.

Similar conditions were found at other plants, but Indorama’s tests showed the worst results.

The public health implications were enormous.

An additional one in every 500 people who lived near the plant for most of their lives was likely to develop cancer from exposure to ethylene oxide, a March 2024 EPA report concluded. That risk is 20 times the 1-in-10,000 level that the E.P.A. typically considers to be the highest acceptable cancer risk when it evaluates carcinogens.

That cancer threat from the Indorama plant could be cut by 95 percent, the E.P.A. found, if better pollution controls were installed.

“There was a sense of urgency,” said Joseph Goffman, who supervised Ms. Shine’s work as the head of the agency’s air office during the Biden administration. “It really alarmed local communities.”

Indorama executives argued that the E.P.A. had gathered samples while the plant was undergoing maintenance, so the results did not reflect normal operations, records show. But when agency inspectors returned in 2024, they still found ethylene oxide leaking in multiple locations and drifting across the facility’s fence line.

A spokeswoman for Indorama declined to address detailed questions from The Times about the plant and cancer risks because they involve continuing regulatory discussions.

“Indorama Ventures recognizes the importance of protecting the health and well-being of our employees, neighbors and surrounding communities,” Patricia Sakamiti, a company spokeswoman, said in a statement.

The test results were a critical factor in the E.P.A.’s approving the new air toxics rules.

Those rules required Indorama and other facilities to limit leaks from valves and upgrade flares so that they could burn off more toxic gases before they were released. The companies also had to install monitors around a plant’s fence line. The results would be publicly posted, letting neighbors see what they were breathing.

The E.P.A. estimated that similar improvements would cost about $440 million to install and $163 million a year to maintain for all affected facilities. That would constitute less than 1 percent of the industry’s national sales.

For that price, millions of people who live near these plants would be at a lower cancer risk, the agency concluded.

Indorama said the E.P.A. had acted “beyond its statutory authority” when it required the fence line tests and that the demands were based on a “flawed risk assessment.” Executives from plants that use ethylene oxide to sterilize medical devices, including the one outside Richmond, joined the protests.

So did companies like U.S. Steel, which operates a facility in Clairton, Pa., near Pittsburgh. The plant bakes coal at up to 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit, turning it into coke, an ingredient in steel making.

U.S. Steel, in a statement at the time, said it was committed to working with the E.P.A. in supporting regulations that were “well grounded in law” and science. “Unfortunately, the 2024 coke rules do not meet these criteria,” it said.

Eleven days into the second Trump administration, Lee Zeldin, the newly sworn-in E.P.A. administrator, received a request from the American Chemistry Council and American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, the two biggest trade groups for the chemical industry.

They wanted Mr. Zeldin, a former Republican lawmaker, to push the president to give them relief from the Biden-era rules.

The trade associations, in their petition, laid the groundwork for the Trump administration to intervene for national security reasons, arguing that the new requirements could cause them to curb or cease production. “National security includes economic security and protection of domestic production of chemicals vital to public health,” the petition said.

The chemical and medical device industries were also busy writing a flurry of checks to Mr. Trump’s causes.

AdvaMed sent $125,000 to his inauguration fund and $1 million to MAGA Inc., one of Mr. Trump’s campaign affiliates. The latter donation was made on the same day in April 2025 that AdvaMed’s chief executive, Scott Whitaker, attended a candlelight dinner with Mr. Trump at his Mar-a-Lago resort.

“Yes, I met with President Trump and was grateful for the opportunity to introduce our lifesaving industry to him,” Mr. Whitaker said in a statement, adding that ethylene oxide did not come up.

One of the E.P.A. officials who was copied on the request for regulatory relief was Mr. Szabo, a senior adviser who was awaiting confirmation to lead the agency’s powerful Office of Air and Radiation, which oversees regulations intended to curb toxic pollution.

In Mr. Trump’s first administration, Mr. Szabo had served as a White House lawyer, helping review new regulations. But before that term ended, he moved to the lobbying world, representing oil and gas companies, chemical manufacturers and coal-burning electric utilities.

His clients included AdvaMed, and Mr. Szabo secured private meetings with the E.P.A. and the White House through 2024 to help the medical device industry fight the Biden-era changes, records show. Before Mr. Trump’s re-election, Mr. Szabo also helped draft the E.P.A. chapter in Project 2025, the conservative blueprint for a second Trump term.

From his new perch within the E.P.A., Mr. Szabo began participating in gatherings at the agency’s headquarters with former clients and working on the industry’s wish list, according to emails reviewed by The Times.

Brigit Hirsch, an E.P.A. spokeswoman, said in a statement that an ethics agreement Mr. Szabo signed last year permitted him to work on “general” matters that affected various industry players but not “particular” matters that narrowly affected his former clients until one year passed.

E.P.A. officials held at least 40 meetings with chemical industry executives in 2025, agency entrance logs show.

Mr. Szabo coordinated these efforts with two deputies who had joined the E.P.A. after stints in industry: Abigale Tardif, a former lobbyist for the oil refiner Marathon Petroleum and American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, and Alexander Dominguez, a former American Petroleum Institute lobbyist.

Mr. Szabo also reached out to Emily Underwood, a senior White House lawyer, suggesting that the president could invoke the Clean Air Act exemptions, documents show.

“Thanks Aaron! Can we just see the copy for POTUS’ proposed mention of/remarks on this?” Ms. Underwood responded.

Ms. Underwood, when reached by phone, told The Times that the agency took the lead on these efforts: “The best person to talk to on that would be Aaron Szabo at the E.P.A.”

Mr. Szabo declined to comment. Ms. Tardif did not respond to requests for comment.

The same day that he corresponded with Ms. Underwood, Mr. Szabo appeared before the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee for his confirmation hearing. It was Ash Wednesday, and Mr. Szabo, a Catholic, bore a cross of ashes on his forehead.

Mr. Szabo told senators that he had a personal stake in clean-air rules because he had cystic fibrosis, a lung disease exacerbated by air pollution.

“Growing up, I could feel the impact of poor air quality in my lungs,” he said.

A week later, the E.P.A. created a special inbox to receive requests for waivers from the rules. Companies soon flooded the agency with submissions.

To understand the newfound power of the chemical industry inside the E.P.A., consider a meeting in May 2025 at the agency’s satellite offices in North Carolina.

Nearly a dozen senior chemical industry executives flew in and gathered in a large conference room. Another 30 industry members joined on a video call. The participants represented some of the industry’s biggest players, including Dow, BASF and Huntsman.

The agenda was set by the chemical industry rather than its regulators.

“To provide some structure to our discussions, we prepared the attached agenda,” Leslie Bellas, a vice president for regulatory affairs at American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, wrote to the E.P.A. team.

The de facto moderator was Brendan Mascarenhas, a lobbyist for the American Chemistry Council, according to meeting minutes and participants.

Industry officials were not shy about their demands then and at follow-up gatherings with E.P.A. officials, the minutes show.

First, they wanted the E.P.A. to rescind its scientific finding that ethylene oxide was much more likely to cause cancer than previously thought. The determination had formed a legal basis for many regulations, and with it gone, the rules would fall like dominoes.

Companies also wanted to roll back requirements for fence line monitors. And in the event of a leak, they wanted to keep plants running longer before shutting down for repairs.

That same month, the chief executives of Dow, Chemours, OxyChem and the American Chemistry Council gathered with Mr. Zeldin at his office in Washington.

Chris Jahn, the head of the chemistry council, wrote on social media afterward that they discussed transforming the E.P.A. so that it focused on “pro-growth policies,” while also “protecting human health and the environment.”

By July 2025, when Mr. Trump had still not granted the waivers, executives grew anxious.

The deadline for the first of the new pollution controls was only a year away, and it would take nearly that long to install the necessary equipment. So the chief executives of Dow, BASF, Eastman Chemical and Huntsman wrote a letter directly to Mr. Trump and shared it with the E.P.A.

“We write to bring to your attention the urgent need for action on requests submitted earlier this year for Presidential Exemptions under the Clean Air Act to provide relief from unnecessary and ineffective obligations imposed by E.P.A.,” they wrote.

Three days later, on July 17, Mr. Trump began answering their pleas.

A series on the Trump administration’s historic weakening of environmental protections, and the resulting increase in air and water pollution.

He issued his first exemptions for 50 chemical plants and 40 sterilizers. His order said that “the current compliance timeline would undermine our national security,” and that the sterilizer rule relied on “technologies that do not exist in a commercially viable form,” even though the breadbox-like enclosures were already in use in some states.

The E.P.A. pointed to Mr. Trump when asked about the exemptions. “This decision was made by the White House, as it is a presidential authority,” Mr. Szabo wrote to one Texas Republican lawmaker.

Then, two of the former lobbyists within the E.P.A. turned to weakening the underlying rules.

One was Ms. Tardif, who had represented the oil refiner Marathon Petroleum in meetings at the E.P.A. as recently as December 2024. In a June 2025 email, an official at American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers thanked her for “productive discussions” about “reconsideration” of the chemical plant rules and copied an official at Marathon.

The other was Mr. Szabo, who asked his staff this spring to strike the same provisions from the sterilizer rule that he had once represented AdvaMed in opposing, including the requirement to install the enclosures.

He delivered an even bigger victory to his former clients by summer.

In a memo dated Aug. 13, E.P.A. staff members warned Mr. Szabo that removing the fence line monitoring requirement for all affected chemical plants would be “difficult to justify” in court. They also noted that the Clean Air Act required the E.P.A. to address “air toxics that pose the greatest potential health threat,” including those tied to cancer.

Despite those warnings, Mr. Szabo issued the order to kill the mandate that same day.

It would be one of Mr. Szabo’s final acts at the agency. This month he resigned and took another job at a law firm that has represented industry groups in their challenges to some of the same Clean Air Act rules.

In Clairton, smokestacks at U.S. Steel’s facility release clouds of steam and chemicals. Thanks to the Trump administration, the plant no longer has to curb some of its toxic emissions, at least for now.

Melanie Meade’s house, in her family for generations, sits on a ridge overlooking the plant. In her backyard, it often smells like rotten eggs or burning rubber, and time outdoors makes her feel lightheaded.

Ms. Meade said she knew she faced an elevated risk of cancer, which killed her older sister and several of her neighbors. But she cannot afford to buy a comparable house elsewhere. So she stays.

A spokesman for U.S. Steel, Andrew Fulton, said in an email that Clairton Coke Works had never been fined for exceeding benzene emissions standards. The company plans to invest up to $2.5 billion in its plants in southwestern Pennsylvania, but none of it will be spent on new pollution controls in Clairton, Mr. Fulton said.

“It would be premature for U.S. Steel or any other regulated company to invest in controls while the rule is under reconsideration,” he said.

In Groves, Texas, which sits adjacent to the Indorama plant, some residents were surprised to learn that Mr. Trump had waived requirements designed to protect their health. Their reactions were mixed.

Chris Borne, the mayor of Groves, appreciates Indorama.

“I have full faith in our facilities where I live,” said Mr. Borne, an electrician who has handled jobs in many of the area’s chemical plants. “Sometimes the rule makers, they go too far.”

Others were angry about the administration’s moves.

“Making things great again — I thought that meant making all things great, including our health,” said Lance Bridges, who voted for Mr. Trump in 2016.

As Mr. Bridges spoke, his 22-year-old daughter pushed a toy scooter carrying his granddaughter in front of their house.

A few weeks later, the Indorama plant had another accidental discharge. Gases started seeping into the community at 6 a.m. on Sept. 11, shortly before students began streaming into school.

State records show that the leak continued for eight hours.

Andrew Chavez and Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: Noah Adams, Longtime Host of ‘All Things Considered,’ Has Died at 84
item.description:
Noah Adams, a longtime host of NPR’s “All Things Considered” whose quiet baritone and empathetic ear brought listeners stories of back-roads America not often heard on the national airwaves, died on Oct. 16 at his home in Yellow Springs, Ohio. He was 84.

The cause was complications of a benign brain tumor removed eight years ago, his wife, Neenah Ellis, said.

Mr. Adams was a postman’s son from Kentucky who never finished college, and he worked hard to lose the Appalachian accent that he knew conjured up negative stereotypes about his native region.

But he never lost his respect for rural and working-class Americans, and he delighted in leaving Washington, where NPR is based, to travel around the country interviewing miners, farmers, single mothers and factory workers.

In the morning meetings, where the day’s events and newsmakers were discussed, Ms. Ellis, who worked in production at NPR, recalled, “He was looking for who was yearning, who was in pain, who needed help out in the country.”

Mr. Adams abhorred interviewing officials with pat talking points, though that was often part of his job as host of the weeknight edition of “All Things Considered,” NPR’s flagship news and interview show, a position he held for 18 years. He preferred to seek out regular people whose lives were affected by national events.

“The best stories come from west of the Potomac,” he once said.

His respect for his sources came through in interviews of those unaccustomed to a microphone.

“He was wonderfully warm and conversational with people,” said Melissa Block, another host of “All Things Considered,” who worked as a producer for Mr. Adams early in her career. “I don’t know that anyone talking with him would think, ‘Oh, the interview is about to start.’ It would just be a conversation.”

From 1982 to 1987, Mr. Adams’s co-host on “All Things Considered” was Susan Stamberg, an emotive, brainy New Yorker. It was a matchup that showed how opposites attract.

“He is the most genuine, uncontrived voice in broadcasting,” Ms. Stamberg wrote in the introduction to a 1992 book that Mr. Adams wrote about a year of his work for NPR.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

After a short hiatus, he returned to host “All Things Considered” with Robert Siegel and Linda Wertheimer from 1989 until 2002.

“He was a very private and shy person,” Mr. Siegel said in an interview.

After Mr. Adams wrote a book about learning to play the piano at 51, “Piano Lessons” (1997), Mr. Siegel recalled Mr. Adams’s distress at realizing that he would have to perform on his book tour: “I watched him at a Borders, and he was terrified. But he loved what he did. He pulled it off very beautifully.”

During his time away from NPR, from 1987 to 1989, Mr. Adams was recruited to host a replacement show for the much-loved “A Prairie Home Companion,” whose creator, Garrison Keillor, had left. The replacement, “Good Evening,” was another folksy variety show broadcast live from a theater in St. Paul, Minn. It was enlivened by Mr. Adams’s essays about the community on the St. Croix River where he had settled, but it struggled to replicate Mr. Keillor’s audience.

The show lasted less than a year, and Mr. Adams announced his departure shortly before it ended. “I never felt people were saying, ‘Gee, that’s not Garrison Keillor,’” he later said somewhat defensively.

Noah Donald Adams was born on Sept. 15, 1942, in Ashland, Ky., the elder of fraternal twin boys. His father, Roy Adams, and his mother, Edith (Wellman) Adams, a secretary, divorced soon after, and Noah and his brother, James, were raised by their mother and maternal grandparents.

Noah graduated from Ashland High School (now Paul G. Blazer High School) and attended Eastern Kentucky State College (now Eastern Kentucky University) for 18 months before being asked to leave because he was living in unauthorized off-campus housing and writing term papers for football players.

He knocked around doing various jobs, — including construction and car sales, before joining the University of Kentucky’s public radio station, WBKY (now WUKY), in Lexington. There, he hosted a progressive rock show and worked the control board for other shows.

After writing a letter to NPR, he was hired in 1975 as a production assistant on “All Things Considered,” which had been introduced four years earlier. In 1978, he became a weekend co-host for the show.

A 90-minute documentary that he co-wrote about the mass suicide at Jonestown in Guyana in 1978, “Father Cares: The Last of Jonestown” (1981), received wide notice for its innovative format and subject. It was based on 900 hours of recordings that the cult leader Jim Jones and his followers had made before their deaths. Mr. Jones’s voice was so chilling, The Minneapolis Star Tribune noted, that “a listener might cling to the rational tone of narrator Noah Adams as to the hand of a friend.”

Though he preferred feature reporting, Mr. Adams did not shy away from hard news at home or abroad. He won an award from the Overseas Press Club of America in 1994 for work he did in Serbia on the roots of the country’s national extremism.

On Sept. 11, 2001, he was on the air from the morning until after dark, updating millions of listeners about the terrorist attacks. He called it the most important day of his career, when he could “feel the audience” intent on understanding the shocking events, Ms. Ellis said.

The following year, Mr. Adams took a leave of absence to research a book about the Wright brothers, one of five nonfiction books he wrote. When he returned, it was as a contributing correspondent on NPR’s national desk. He roamed widely but regularly returned to stories in Appalachia.

Ms. Ellis, who married Mr. Adams in 1987, recalled visiting Appalachia for the first time with him. They were on assignment — she was his producer — and he instructed her and an engineer on how to approach strangers wary of outsiders. You don’t knock on their doors, he told them: “You drive up, get out of the car and stand there until they come out.”

Mr. Adams’s first two marriages ended in divorce. In addition to Ms. Ellis, he is survived by his brother.

Among the thousands of stories that Mr. Adams reported, the one that got the most enthusiastic response was when he visited a New York recording studio and sang a wobbly version of the Eagles song “Take It to the Limit.”

He played the tape on the air for Ms. Stamberg, who squealed, “It’s adorable!”

One of the hundreds of listeners who wrote in said, “I was getting ready to drop out of law school and we were thinking about getting a divorce, but if you have the courage to stand in that studio and play it for Susan on the radio, then I know we can do anything we really set our minds to.”

item.title: Six Flags Will Add Seatbelts to Some Roller Coasters After Rider’s Death
item.description:
Six Flags will add seatbelts to select roller coasters across its parks, the company said on Friday, weeks after the death of a man who fell from a ride at one of its properties.

The announcement came as Six Flags contended with recent lawsuits over safety concerns.

John Reilly, the president of Six Flags Entertainment Corporation, said in a statement on Friday that the company’s parks hired independent engineers and inspectors to conduct safety reviews of all rides and attractions as the additional safety measures were put in place.

“We are committed to carefully evaluating their findings and taking appropriate action to further strengthen our standards and culture of safety,” Mr. Reilly said in the statement.

Earlier this month, Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was thrown from his seat and declared dead after riding Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia in Austell, Ga., the state’s tallest roller coaster. That ride is temporarily closed and will receive seatbelts when it reopens.

Goliath was previously equipped with the commonly used lap-bar “clamshell” restraints, which swing down to lock above the riders’ laps.

State authorities, as well as the Cobb County Police Department, are investigating the death, but there is no single federal agency responsible for enforcing safety standards for rides like Goliath, which had passed its most recent state inspection on March 16.

The other attractions that will receive the safety additions are Nitro at Six Flags Great Adventure in Jackson, N.J., and Raging Bull at Six Flags Great America in Gurnee, Ill., which is north of Chicago, a spokeswoman for the company said in an email on Saturday.

Aside from Goliath, eight rides at five other parks are temporarily closed, Mr. Reilly said in his statement.

Ride safety at Six Flags parks has come under intense scrutiny over the past several weeks, even before Mr. Kariem’s death.

In September, three people sued the amusement park company and the ride’s manufacturer after suffering what they said were catastrophic brain injuries from riding the X2 coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California. The lawsuits accuse Six Flags and a manufacturer of X2’s parts of operating a defectively designed ride and failing to adequately warn passengers about the risk of serious brain injuries.

That month, Six Flags Magic Mountain said the X2 would permanently close.

Before those lawsuits, Mr. Reilly said during an August call with analysts that the company incurred higher repair and maintenance expenses at certain parks as it reduced downtime, adding, “We will not compromise on safety.”

In its second-quarter financial filings, released in August, Six Flags reported that its net revenue was $865 million, a decrease of $65 million from the same time last year. Attendance for the quarter was just above 13 million visits, a decrease from more than 14 million for the same period in 2025.

There are currently more than 220 coasters operating across all Six Flags parks, Mr. Reilly said on Friday.

“We will continue to communicate about our progress and hold ourselves accountable to our commitments to you,” he said.

item.title: Audi to Build Factory in Georgia, Trump Says
item.description:
Audi, Volkswagen’s luxury car division, plans to build a factory in Georgia, its first in the United States, President Trump said at a rally in the state on Saturday.

A factory in the United States would help Volkswagen and Audi reduce their exposure to Mr. Trump’s 25 percent import tariffs on foreign vehicles and auto parts that have been deadly for sales. Audi imports all the vehicles it sells in the United States from factories in Europe or Mexico.

Volkswagen has a factory in Chattanooga, Tenn., but produces only one model there, the Atlas sport utility vehicle. Other Volkswagen models are imported, in many cases from Mexico.

Audi will invest $4 billion in the factory south of Macon, which will be able to produce 200,000 vehicles a year, Georgia officials said. Audi will begin grading earth at the site this year but it will not reach full production until 2031.

Mr. Trump portrayed the investment as a sign that his tariffs, which economists have said are inflationary, had inspired Audi’s decision. “Without tariffs, they would not have been coming in,” Mr. Trump said.

Audi will produce sport utility vehicles at the site, Gernot Döllner, the head of Audi, said after being called to the stage by Mr. Trump.

BMW and Mercedes-Benz, Audi’s main rivals, have long had factories in the United States — BMW in South Carolina and Mercedes in Alabama — where they mainly produce sport utility vehicles.

By promising to invest in a key battleground state, and giving Mr. Trump something to brag about, Volkswagen may be hoping to win concessions from the White House that would lower the tariff burden and help the company revive flagging sales in the United States.

“We can do something with you because you’re building your cars in the United States,” Mr. Trump said.

Sales of Volkswagen cars in the United States, including the Audi and Porsche brands, slumped almost 10 percent in the third quarter, according to estimates by Cox Automotive. With a market share of 3.4 percent, Volkswagen is a minor player in the United States even though it is the second-largest carmaker worldwide after Toyota.

The German carmaker has been trying for decades to increase its sales in the United States to a level commensurate with its global stature. The United States is particularly attractive because it is one of the few markets where there is no competition from Chinese carmakers. Chinese cars are effectively barred from the United States by tariffs of more than 100 percent.

Volkswagen is already building a factory in South Carolina to manufacture pickups and sport utility vehicles using the Scout brand beginning next year.

Such projects are risky. Automakers including Volkswagen are already burdened with underused factories that weigh on profits. Volkswagen, which has lost market share in Europe to Chinese automakers like BYD and Geely, has said that it may need to close or sell four factories in Europe.

Richard Fausset contributed reporting.
